title: Latency-Utility Token Allocator — whiteboard notes
content:
Purpose:
This note captures a lightweight, sketched design for a scheduler that uses a latency-utility function to decide how to aggregate tokens into GPU execution batches while preserving per-request fairness and KV-cache locality. The goal is a practical allocator we can prototype in the runtime agent today without large refactors.

Background / motivation:
- Existing continuous batchers are either token-first (optimize kernel utilization by merging tokens aggressively) or request-first (respect request latency budgets). Both extremes have failure modes: token-first starves low-rate, latency-sensitive requests; request-first reduces throughput and wastes kernel opportunities.
- We need a middle path: a scheduler that optimizes a utility function combining latency impact, throughput gain (per-token marginal utility), and KV cache affinity penalty.

High-level idea:
- Compute a small per-request urgency score on arrival: U_req = base_priority + (T_budget - elapsed) / T_budget_factor.
- For each candidate mergeable token group, compute marginal utility MU = expected_token_throughput_gain - latency_cost_adjustment.
- Latency-utility for a potential merge is: LUtil = sum_over_requests(U_req * delta_latency_request) + alpha * (-total_kernel_cost_reduction) + beta * KV_affinity_adjustment. We schedule merges with the most negative LUtil (largest net win) subject to a max-latency constraint per request.

Key signals and approximations (cheap to compute):
- expected_token_throughput_gain: microbench lookup by (model, seq_len_bucket, kernel_variant) -> predicted tokens/s improvement if we batch n_tokens. We maintain a small heatmap (256 buckets) updated from telemetry.
- delta_latency_request: predicted increase in tail latency for that request if it waits one more batch window. Approximated by measured per-request percentiles and a simple linear extrapolation.
- KV_affinity_adjustment: small penalty if tokens being merged have heterogeneous KV keys and thus will reduce cache hit rate. Estimate via intersection cardinality of top-K keys in requests (cheap bloom-filters).
- kernel warmup penalty: if choosing a different kernel_variant (e.g., FP16->int8 or a different cuBLAS path) the first few micro-batches pay a setup penalty; factor into MU.

Fairness mechanics (token-level vs request-level):
- Per-request latency budgets enforced as hard constraints: never schedule a merge that causes any request to exceed max_budget (user-specified per-route SLOs).
- Within the feasible set, prefer merges that improve a weighted per-request utility: each request gets a decaying virtual-age credit; long-waiting low-throughput requests gain higher U_req so they get merged sooner.
- This is effectively a hybrid: token-level pooling for throughput when utility positive; request-level protection via budgets & virtual-age fairness.

Pseudocode sketch:
- On arrival: compute U_req and insert into open_requests set.
- Periodic (every 1-3ms) window: collect head tokens across open_requests that are eligible to merge (same model/shard).
- For k in 1..K (small): propose candidate merges by combining top-k tokens sorted by U_req but reject if max_budget_violation. Compute LUtil for candidate; pick candidate with lowest LUtil < threshold. Execute merge -> dispatch kernel. Update virtual ages.

KV cache affinity handling:
- Store lightweight fingerprint per request (e.g., 64-bit bloom sketch of top KV keys). When considering merges, compute an overlap score. Penalize merges that reduce expected KV hit rate below a threshold, especially for long-context requests that will suffer large retrieval costs.
- If a request has high KV affinity to a single worker, prefer local scheduling (soft affinity) to avoid cross-worker cache misses.

Kernel selection and warm starts:
- Maintain a per-model kernel profile: for each kernel variant, store tokens/s and a cold-start penalty. The allocator should consider switching kernel variants only when MU(net gain) > warmup_penalty * hysteresis_factor.
- Prefer stable variants for small merges; be opportunistic for large merges.

Metrics and heuristics to track (telemetry):
- per-batch tokens/s, kernel_variant, merge_size distribution
- per-request wait_time distribution and percentiles by route
- KV cache hit rate pre/post merge
- cases where per-request budget would be violated (debug tracer)

Microbench plan / experiment matrix:
- Simulated traffic mixes: 90/9/1 (small chat/medium batch/long context), varying arrival rates and SLOs.
- Grid over alpha, beta (utility weighting) and virtual-age decay to find Pareto frontier of latency vs throughput.
- Evaluate: p50/p95 latency per route, aggregate tokens/s, KV hit-rate delta, fairness metric (max - min per-request slowdown).

Open questions / tradeoffs:
- How expensive is bloom-intersection at 1–2ms decision windows? Might need to sample or approximate via precomputed locality buckets.
- Is the utility function convex/monotonic? If not, greedy picks may be locally bad. Add a small randomized exploration to avoid local minima.
- Interaction with autoscaler: batching can change throughput profile dramatically; coordinate with capacity planning to avoid oscillation.
- Do we allow preemption of a kernel execution to serve an urgent request? Currently no; preemption is high-cost. Explore tiny reserved slots for ultra-low-latency requests.

Implementation notes / rollout plan:
- Phase 1: implement allocator as a best-effort module that runs in the dispatcher, returns merge decisions; keep existing continuous batcher as fallback. Feature-flagged.
- Phase 2: add KV fingerprint sketches and integrate kernel heatmap metrics. Run parallel A/B with telemetry collection.
- Phase 3: expose route-level policy knobs (max_budget, alpha/beta) and a per-customer SLA override.

Immediate TODOs (next 2 sprints):
- Diego: prototype small utility evaluator that consumes existing kernel heatmap (SRV-1423).
- Priya: design compact KV fingerprint format and microbench bloom intersection cost.
- Evan: simulation harness (3 synthetic mixes) and automated sweep over alpha/beta.
- Me (Aisha): write a small API spec for dispatcher <-> allocator interactions and add feature flag in runtime config.

Notes / references:
- See linked Linear ticket SRV-1423 for initial heatmap telemetry work.
- Related design: request-hedging work in PR 916 (different focus but useful for fallback behavior).

Closing thought:
This approach is intentionally pragmatic: a small, explainable utility function that blends latency protection, throughput opportunity, and KV locality. If the prototype shows predictable benefits we can evolve toward more statistical learners, but start simple so operators can reason about knobs.
